Patients are either on stable treatment* with nintedanib therapy for at least 12 weeks and plan to stay on this background treatment after randomisation, or not on treatment with nintedanib for at least 8 weeks (eg, either antifibrotic treatment naïve or previously discontinued) and do not plan to start or restart antifibrotic treatment. Patients treated with permitted immunosuppressive agents (other than corticosteroids) for an underlying systemic disease (eg, methotrexate, azathioprine) need to be on a stable treatment for at least 12 weeks prior to visit 1 and during the screening period. Exclusion criteria Patients treated with the following medications prior to visit 1: Oral corticosteroids >15 mg/day within 4 weeks. Cyclophosphamide, tocilizumab or mycophenolate within 8 weeks. Rituximab within 6 months. Prebronchodilator FEV 1 /FVC <0.7 at visit 1. Patients with an acute ILD exacerbation within 3 months and/or during the screening period. Active, unstable or uncontrolled vasculitis within 8 weeks. Any suicidal behaviour (past 2 years) or suicidal ideation of type 4 or 5 on the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (past 3 months). *Stable therapy is defined as a tolerated regimen of nintedanib (no dose change) for at least 12 weeks. DLco, diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide; FEV 1 , forced expiratory volume in 1 s; FVC, forced vital capacity; HRCT, high-resolution CT; ILD, interstitial lung disease; IPF, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Outcomes The primary endpoint is absolute change from baseline in FVC (mL) at week 52. Other endpoints are shown in . Box 2 Endpoints Primary endpoint Absolute change from baseline in FVC (mL) at week 52. Key secondary endpoint Time to first acute ILD exacerbation, first respiratory hospitalisation or death (whichever occurs first) over the duration of the trial. Other secondary endpoints Time to first acute ILD exacerbation or death over the duration of the trial. Time to hospitalisation for respiratory cause or death over the duration of the trial. Time to absolute decline in FVC% predicted of >10% from baseline or death over the duration of the trial. Time to absolute decline in DLco% predicted of >15% from baseline or death over the duration of the trial. Time to death over the duration of the trial. Absolute change from baseline in L-PF Symptoms dyspnoea domain score at week 52. Absolute change from baseline in L-PF Symptoms cough domain score at week 52. Absolute change from baseline in L-PF Symptoms fatigue domain score at week 52. Absolute change from baseline in FVC% predicted at week 52. Absolute change from baseline in DLco% predicted at week 52. DLco, diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide; FVC, forced vital capacity; ILD, interstitial lung disease; L-PF, living with pulmonary fibrosis. Patient-reported outcome measures will include the Living with Pulmonary Fibrosis Symptoms and Impact questionnaire total scores, EuroQol 5-Dimensional Quality of Life questionnaire total scores and the Patient’s Global Impression of Severity for Cough, Shortness of Breath and Fatigue. Pharmacokinetic endpoints include predose plasma concentrations of BI 1015550. Exploratory biomarkers of inflammation, epithelial injury, tissue degradation and fibrosis will be assessed in blood over time ( ). Safety Adverse events will be coded using the Medical Dictionary for Drug Regulatory Activities. An independent data monitoring committee (DMC) that is unblinded to the treatment allocation will monitor the safety and progress of the trial. Safety monitoring and analyses will include physical examination, vital signs, safety laboratory parameters, ECG, review of adverse events reporting, Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale. Adverse events of special interest, which include potential severe drug-induced liver injury, vasculitis, severe infections, new onset of severe depression or new onset of severe anxiety, will be monitored. Statistical analysis The primary endpoint of absolute change from baseline in FVC (mL) at week 52 will be estimated using a mixed-effect model for repeated measures analysis. This model will include discrete fixed effects for treatment at each visit, baseline intake of nintedanib therapy at each visit, HRCT pattern at each visit and continuous fixed effects for baseline FVC (mL) value at each visit. The key secondary endpoint will be analysed using a Cox proportional hazards model with data from the whole trial (ie, including data beyond 52 weeks). The model will include treatment, HRCT pattern, background nintedanib treatment, age, FVC% predicted and diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide % predicted (corrected for haemoglobin) at baseline as covariates. To account for multiplicity introduced by testing two doses of BI 1015550 vs placebo for the primary and key secondary endpoints, the graphical testing procedure as depicted in will be used to maintain the family-wise type I error rate at a two-sided alpha level of 0.05. The trial plans to randomise 1041

a Cox proportional hazards model with data from the whole trial (ie, including data beyond 52 weeks). The model will include treatment, HRCT pattern, background nintedanib treatment, age, FVC% predicted and diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide % predicted (corrected for haemoglobin) at baseline as covariates. To account for multiplicity introduced by testing two doses of BI 1015550 vs placebo for the primary and key secondary endpoints, the graphical testing procedure as depicted in will be used to maintain the family-wise type I error rate at a two-sided alpha level of 0.05. The trial plans to randomise 1041 patients so that 347 patients are included in each study arm. Approximately 30% of patients are expected to be on background nintedanib treatment. This corresponds to the current treatment/prescription practices across the participating countries. This sample size will provide approximately 90% power to detect a treatment effect of 71 mL in change from baseline in FVC at week 52 for at least one dose group with an overall type I error of 0.05. For the primary endpoint, statistical significance will be declared if the analyses in either dose group are statistically significant at the designated alpha level according to . The assumed treatment effect of 71 mL was derived based on the assumed FVC decline at week 52 in the placebo arm taking into account the expected number of patients with background nintedanib use, different HRCT patterns (usual interstitial pneumonia-like vs other fibrotic patterns) and FVC changes observed in INPULSIS and INBUILD. Intercurrent events (except for death and lung transplant) will be handled via a treatment policy strategy. Missing data will not be imputed except for death, where a poor outcome will be assigned. Lung transplant will be handled via a hypothetical strategy. Data measured after a patient’s lung transplantation will be censored. The mixed-effect model will handle missing data based on a likelihood method under the ‘missing at random assumption’. A tipping point analysis is planned as sensitivity analysis to assess the robustness of the primary analysis against deviations from the missing at random assumption. The effect of missing data on the primary endpoint will be further investigated using other multiple imputation techniques. Sensitivity analyses, including different covariates in the primary analysis model, will also be performed. Appropriate sample and data management system for clinical data and samples is in place, and patient identification numbers will be used to ensure confidentiality. The investigator or institution will allow site trial-related monitoring, audits, institutional review boards/independent ethics committees review and regulatory inspections. Trial governance and oversight An independent DMC that is unblinded to the treatment allocation will primarily evaluate safety data and limited efficacy data on a regular basis. An interim analysis to assess the futility of the 9 mg BID dose will be performed by the independent DMC when approximately 300 patients in the trial (100 patients per arm) have completed 12 weeks of treatment. The independent DMC will make a recommendation to the sponsor on the continuation or stoppage of the 9 mg BID dose arm. The same independent DMC will review the sister trial in IPF (FIBRONEER-IPF) to ensure the broadest possible evaluation of safety in the programme. An independent adjudication committee composed of cardiologists and neurologists will review all fatal cases for the primary cause of death and all adverse events categorised as major adverse cardiovascular events. A separate independent adjudication committee composed of rheumatologists/vasculitis experts will review all events of suspected or possible vasculitis. A contingency plan has been developed for this trial in case patients are not able to perform an on-site visit due to their health status or COVID-19, which includes the direct shipment of investigational products to patients, remote check-ups and home spirometry. Patients and public involvement During the planning of the FIBRONEER trials, feedback on the trial designs was obtained from a trial simulation involving patients, caregivers and healthcare professionals and during advisory board meetings with members of patient organisations and ILD experts. Participants provided their insights on the trial design, trial assessments, trial visit schedule and duration, and participant support. Patient-focused adaptations were then made to the trial protocols and conduct. Ethics and dissemination The trial is being conducted in compliance with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, in accordance with the International Council on Harmonisation Guideline for Good Clinical Practice, the EU directive 2001/20/EC and the Japanese Good Clinical Practice regulations (Ministry of Health and Welfare Ordinance No. 28, 27 March 1997). Written informed consent will be obtained from each patient before entry into the study. Collection of blood samples for DNA banking is optional and not a prerequisite for participation (only for patients who have signed a separate informed consent form). Samples may be analysed retrospectively. The study results will be disseminated at scientific congresses and in

with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, in accordance with the International Council on Harmonisation Guideline for Good Clinical Practice, the EU directive 2001/20/EC and the Japanese Good Clinical Practice regulations (Ministry of Health and Welfare Ordinance No. 28, 27 March 1997). Written informed consent will be obtained from each patient before entry into the study. Collection of blood samples for DNA banking is optional and not a prerequisite for participation (only for patients who have signed a separate informed consent form). Samples may be analysed retrospectively. The study results will be disseminated at scientific congresses and in peer-reviewed publications. Discussion The FIBRONEER-ILD trial is evaluating the efficacy, safety and tolerability of BI 1015550 compared with placebo in patients with PPF in addition to patient’s standard of care over at least 52 weeks. A sister phase III study, FIBRONEER-IPF, is being conducted in parallel in patients with IPF. Together, these studies aim to address the need for new treatments for pulmonary fibrosis. Selection of patients with PPF The phase II trial of BI 1015550 was conducted in patients with IPF, and no data exist for patients with PPF. However, in patients with PPF, the natural history appears to follow a course similar to IPF, with worsening of respiratory symptoms, lung function decline, reduced quality of life and early mortality. Nintedanib is approved for both IPF and PPF based on similar clinical outcomes and consistent effects in both diseases. Together, this suggests shared underlying pathobiological mechanisms in patients with IPF and PPF. Given the positive efficacy and tolerability results in the phase II trial in IPF, it is hypothesised that similar treatment effects may be seen in patients with PPF. Furthermore, due to the rare nature of many ILD diagnoses, the grouping of patients with different ILDs that demonstrate PPF behaviour provides an opportunity to conduct an appropriately powered clinical study that is reflective of a real-world population. This grouping is similar to that used in the INBUILD trial, and is justified based on their clinical and biological similarities. Targeting inflammation and fibrosis ILDs incorporate a wide range of lung disorders, characterised by parenchymal damage mediated by inflammation and fibrosis. PDE4 inhibition is being used in inflammatory diseases such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and psoriasis. Many lung diseases that manifest PPF also have an inflammatory component, including fibrotic connective tissue disease-associated ILD, fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis and idiopathic non-specific interstitial pneumonia. PDE4 inhibition produces anti-inflammatory effects by reducing the release of proinflammatory mediators and reducing the recruitment of inflammatory cells. Preclinical evidence has also shown that PDE4 inhibitors are associated with antifibrotic effects and may reduce fibrotic remodelling in lung disease. In preclinical studies, BI 1015550 has demonstrated anti-inflammatory and antifibrotic effects in in vitro and in vivo models of lung fibrosis. Rationale for including patients with and without background nintedanib In preclinical studies, the combination of nintedanib and BI 1015550 demonstrated potentially synergistic effects on the inhibition of fibroblast proliferation in primary lung fibroblasts in patients with IPF. In the phase II trial, treatment with BI 1015550 at 18 mg BID preserved lung function in patients with IPF over the 12-week study period in patients either receiving or not receiving antifibrotic therapy, with suggestion of an additive effect with nintedanib. Predose and postdose concentration levels of BI 1015550 were similar between patients treated with nintedanib and those not treated with any antifibrotics, indicating that nintedanib use did not impact the exposure of BI 1015550. Thus, the efficacy and safety of BI 1015550 will be assessed in patients with PPF with or without background nintedanib treatment. Rationale for dose selection The selection of the BI 1015550 18 mg BID dose is supported by the results from the phase II study, where BI 1015550 treatment preserved lung function in patients with IPF. In this phase III trial, we have an additional 9 mg BID dose to evaluate the benefit–risk profile at a lower dose, as well as to provide further dose-response and exposure-response data. An interim futility analysis is planned to assess the efficacy and safety profile of the 9 mg BID dose, ensuring patients are exposed to the lower dose for the shortest period possible in case of a non-favourable benefit–risk profile. Rationale for the choice of inclusion and exclusion criteria This study opted for similar criteria to the INBUILD trial, given its successful use in a large sample of patients with fibrosing lung disease. The study protocol was developed prior to the American Thoracic Society/European Respiratory Society/Japanese Respiratory Society/Latin American Thorax Association 2022 guidelines on definition of PPF. Although there are minor differences between this definition and the INBUILD criteria, the inclusion criteria used in this trial are inclusive of a broad population of patients with PPF. There is no upper limit for age or FVC, and patients

non-favourable benefit–risk profile. Rationale for the choice of inclusion and exclusion criteria This study opted for similar criteria to the INBUILD trial, given its successful use in a large sample of patients with fibrosing lung disease. The study protocol was developed prior to the American Thoracic Society/European Respiratory Society/Japanese Respiratory Society/Latin American Thorax Association 2022 guidelines on definition of PPF. Although there are minor differences between this definition and the INBUILD criteria, the inclusion criteria used in this trial are inclusive of a broad population of patients with PPF. There is no upper limit for age or FVC, and patients will be included if they have FVC% predicted of ≥45%, which may be more representative of patients with PPF in the real world. Certain immunosuppressive agents that may impact FVC (eg, cyclophosphamide, tocilizumab, mycophenolate, rituximab) will not be allowed in this study, to avoid the potential confounding impact of these drugs on the assessment of the efficacy and safety of BI 1015550 in PPF. Rationale for trial endpoints The study endpoints are consistent with previous trials and reflect clinically meaningful outcomes. In this study, the primary endpoint is absolute change from baseline in FVC (mL) at week 52. This differs from the primary endpoint of annual rate of decline in FVC (mL/year) used in the INBUILD trial due to findings from the phase II study of BI 1015550 in patients with IPF; the phase II study showed an early increase in FVC in the treated group, suggesting a non-linear course. In contrast, a continuous decline was observed with nintedanib in INBUILD. Thus, change from baseline FVC (mL) may be a more suitable endpoint for this phase III study. The short duration of the phase II study and its small sample size limit the conclusions that can be drawn regarding the treatment effect of 18 mg BID. In this phase III trial, the minimum treatment period of 52 weeks has been selected according to the guidance from American and European clinician organisations (2015 American Thoracic Society/European Respiratory Society/Japanese Respiratory Society/Latin American Thorax Association guidelines) to confirm these treatment effects on FVC over a longer time period and in a larger sample of patients. This study also includes a variable period in which patients will continue treatment with BI 1015550 or placebo beyond week 52. Patients with PPF may have different underlying pathophysiology to those with IPF. Thus, there may be heterogeneity in rates of progression and response to treatment throughout the trial. This time scale will also allow more time and longer follow-up, to record more events for the assessment of the key secondary endpoint (time to first exacerbation, hospitalisation due to respiratory cause or death), thus increasing the power of the trial. In addition, specific efficacy and safety endpoints and changes in clinically significant outcomes may vary in occurrence and may only become apparent beyond 52 weeks. Safety assessments Depression and suicidal ideation or behaviour are listed as side effects associated with marketed oral pan-PDE4 inhibitors, and therefore, will be monitored as part of the safety assessments in this trial. In preclinical toxicology studies, PDE4 inhibitors have been associated with vasculitis. In the phase II study, there was one patient with suspected vasculitis and IPF exacerbation, but vasculitis was not confirmed by the independent DMC. Patients will be monitored for vasculitis during this trial and suspected cases will be assessed by the independent adjudication committee and independent DMC. Limitations While some immunosuppressive agents (eg, methotrexate, azathioprine) will be permitted, cyclophosphamide, tocilizumab, mycophenolate, rituximab and high-dose steroids will not be allowed in this study, to avoid the potential confounding impact of these drugs on the assessment of the efficacy and safety of BI 1015550 in PPF. This is a limitation of the trial, as many patients with PPF may use these immunosuppressive agents and biologics in real-world practice. Conclusions The FIBRONEER-ILD trial is investigating the efficacy, safety and tolerability of oral BI 1015550 in patients with PPF, over a long-term period, in patients with or without nintedanib. The study commenced in October 2022. Following the positive results of the BI 1015550 phase II trial in patients with IPF and the similarities in disease course between IPF and PPF, it is anticipated that treatment effects may also be seen in patients with PPF.

documents.title: ACR guideline for treatment of inflammatory myositis adult and juvenile

chunks.content: Introduction Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM) are classically defined as a heterogeneous group of diseases primarily characterized by the common feature of immune-mediated inflammation of muscle fibers and surrounding tissues. The annual incidence of IIM ranges from 0.2 to 2 per 100,000 person-years, with a prevalence ranging from 2 to 25 per 100,000 people. However, these systemic diseases can manifest with a combination of inflammatory muscle, skin, lung, and joint disease. Using clinical features, serology, and muscle pathology, currently, six main phenotypes have been described in adults. Each phenotype has a distinct typical presentation. ( ) Dermatomyositis (DM)- classical skin findings with muscle weakness. A subgroup of patients has skin findings with no clinical muscle disease and are characterized as clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis (CADM). Antisynthetase syndrome (ASyS)- presence of anti-aminoacyl transfer RNA (tRNA) synthetase antibodies (ASAs) with interstitial lung disease (ILD), inflammatory myopathy, arthritis, and/or mechanic’s hands. Overlap myositis (OM)- inflammatory myopathy with simultaneous presence of features of other autoimmune diseases such as systemic sclerosis (SSc), mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD), or Sjögren’s syndrome. Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) - myopathy with muscle biopsy features of myonecrosis without significant inflammatory cells. Inclusion body myositis (IBM) - asymmetric myopathy at disease onset presenting with distal muscle weakness. Muscle biopsy demonstrates endomysial inflammatory infiltrate and muscle fibers with rimmed vacuoles and eosinophilic muscle fiber inclusions. Polymyositis - myositis with the absence of features that would classify patients in the other subgroups. IIMs can affect multiple compartments of the respiratory system including lung parenchyma resulting in ILD, pulmonary vasculature leading to pulmonary hypertension (PH), and respiratory muscles. Aspiration pneumonitis/pneumonia from dysphagia is also seen. ILD is the most common pulmonary manifestation, with an overall estimated prevalence of 40 - 50%. However, in patients with CADM and ASyS the prevalence is over 80%. ILD in IIM can be progressive and carries high morbidity and mortality. This review will discuss pulmonary and extrapulmonary clinical manifestations of IIM-ILD, diagnostic work-up, treatment options, management approach and future directions. We focus on ASyS and DM, which most commonly involve the lungs, however the principles can apply to any phenotype of IIM lung disease. Pathobiology The underlying mechanism of IIM is postulated to be chronic inflammation caused by both innate and adaptive immune activation triggered by interactions between genetic and environmental risk factors ( ). Several HLA and non-HLA genetic associations have been demonstrated in IIM. , Epidemiologic studies have reported numerous environmental risk factors including smoking. Preceding respiratory and gastrointestinal infections - including COVID19 infection have been associated with IIM onset. - Medications such as statins, immune check point inhibitors, d-penicillamine, interferons, and anti-tumor necrosis factor agents are also potential triggers. - A seasonal distribution associated with increased ultraviolet radiation exposure is reported in anti-Jo-1 antibody IIM. , ASyS is characterized by the development of autoantibodies directed against different tRNA-synthetase enzymes. In genetically susceptible individuals, activation of adaptive immune cells and tolerance breakdown leads to antigen presentation, CD8-T cell priming, and CD4-T cell-B cell crosstalk. Release of type I/II interferons, B lymphocyte stimulator, and other cytokines lead to the production of anti-tRNA synthetase autoantibodies. - The resultant aberrant immune activation of T cells, including CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, is thought to play a central role in disease pathogenesis. Activated CD8+ T cells release granzyme B, which cleaves several aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases in the lungs. Active T/B cells and autoantibodies enter the systemic circulation and encounter the altered autoantigens in the lungs, resulting in lung injury. Of the twenty known aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, antibodies against ten have been identified. The most common is anti-histidyl-tRNA-synthetase antibody or anti-Jo-1 antibody. MDA5 is an intracellular protein that helps recognize viral RNA as danger signals. Viral infections might incite autoimmunity through several possible mechanisms. Viral induced MDA5 activation followed by excessive cellular apoptosis could lead to a tolerance breach and development of disease. , Clinical presentation and diagnostic testing The classical presentation of IIM includes a combination of muscle, skin, lung, and joint disease. However, patients may initially manifest symptoms affecting any of these systems in isolation. The disease can become progressive and affect other organs after initial presentation. A multidisciplinary collaboration between pulmonology, rheumatology, dermatology, and neurology plays an important role in the diagnosis and management of these patients, particularly when they do not present with muscle weakness. Serology (<xref rid="T1" ref-type="table">Table 1</xref>) Autoantibodies in IIM are closely linked to clinical phenotypes. In patients with suspected IIM-ILD, antibody testing can help establish a diagnosis. The group of antibodies specific for IIM manifestations are known as myositis-specific antibodies (MSA) and those frequently found in other connective tissue diseases (CTD), which can also cause myositis, are grouped into myositis-associated antibodies (MAA). MSAs include antibodies for DM (Anti-MDA5, Mi-2, TIF-1γ, NXP-2, SAE), ASyS (anti-Jo-1, EJ, OJ, PL-7, PL-12, Ha, Zo, Ks), IMNM (Anti-HMGCR and anti-SRP Ab) and IBM

Serology (<xref rid="T1" ref-type="table">Table 1</xref>) Autoantibodies in IIM are closely linked to clinical phenotypes. In patients with suspected IIM-ILD, antibody testing can help establish a diagnosis. The group of antibodies specific for IIM manifestations are known as myositis-specific antibodies (MSA) and those frequently found in other connective tissue diseases (CTD), which can also cause myositis, are grouped into myositis-associated antibodies (MAA). MSAs include antibodies for DM (Anti-MDA5, Mi-2, TIF-1γ, NXP-2, SAE), ASyS (anti-Jo-1, EJ, OJ, PL-7, PL-12, Ha, Zo, Ks), IMNM (Anti-HMGCR and anti-SRP Ab) and IBM (Anti-cN1A). MAA include antibodies such as anti-PM/Scl, anti-U1RNP, anti-U3RNP, anti-Ku, and anti-Ro52. Several single and multiplex commercial assays are available for detecting the majority of MSAs. These assays include enzyme-linked Immunosorbent assays, addressable laser bead Immunoassays, immunoblotting techniques, and RNA or protein radio-immunoprecipitation. Currently, the gold standard for myositis autoantibody testing is the radio-immunoprecipitation assay. Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) testing is often used to “screen” for CTD. However, it is not useful for detecting the presence of an MSA. Indirect Immunofluorescence using human epithelial type 2 cells as a substrate is the standard screening for ANA with quantification of the titer and ANA staining pattern. Most MSAs will yield a negative ANA result and thus a negative ANA does not rule out ASyS. We suggest starting with a panel that includes all eight available ASAs, anti-MDA-5, and anti-Ro52, which are antibodies that have been associated with ILD. Other antibodies such as anti-HMGCR, anti-SRP, or anti-CN1A can be ordered if clinically indicated. MSA-negative IIM-ILD Patients may present with clinical features consistent with IIM-ILD without myositis-specific autoantibodies. Within this group, those with ILD as the first clinical manifestation represent a more challenging subgroup that requires evaluation by a multidisciplinary team of experts in IIM-ILD. Currently, standard assays only identify the eight most common ASAs that have been associated with IIM-ILD. However, there are other tRNA synthetases whose corresponding autoantibodies are not yet identified by standard assays. Immunoprecipitation is particularly useful in this population of MSA-negative IIM-ILD patients, as it may reveal an immunoprecipitation band representing an unidentified autoantibody. In our practice, we have observed that a significant number of MSA-negative patients have a positive anti-Ro-52 autoantibody. Sclafani et al. reported that 50 ILD patients with only a positive anti-Ro-52 autoantibody had similar outcomes compared to those with co-positivity of anti-Ro-52 and an MSA. This highlights the potential role of the anti-Ro-52 autoantibody in the evaluation of patients with suspected IIM-ILD, particularly those with negative MSA. These patients exhibit a higher mean percent-predicted FVC and lower total HRCT scores compared to patients with the anti-Jo1 autoantibody. Yoshifuji et al. reported that MSA-negative patients had similar lung function, lower ILD recurrence, and a lower response to steroids compared to those who tested positive for Larger studies and the use of novel immunoassays that can detect other ASA will help to better characterize this group. Pulmonary Manifestations Interstitial lung disease - ILD is the most common pulmonary manifestation of IIM, affecting over 80% of patients with ASyS and anti-MDA5. - . In other IIM subtypes, ILD is less prevalent, milder, and often presents with muscle disease. Lung disease preceding extra pulmonary symptoms is seen in 16-65 % of patients, often by several months. Three distinct clinical presentations of IIM-ILD are frequently encountered: Rapidly progressive ILD (RP-ILD) can be seen in an acute exacerbation of previously undiagnosed ILD or in patients with significant worsening of ILD within three months of diagnosis. Acute hypoxic respiratory failure is commonly associated with anti-MDA5 DM and ASyS, particularly anti-Jo1, anti-PL7 and anti-PL12 antibodies. Development of spontaneous pneumomediastinum is a sign of poor prognosis. Chronic ILD (C-ILD) manifests as insidious onset of dyspnea and cough, which can be associated with extra-pulmonary symptoms of IIM. It is the most common presentation in ASyS patients. Sub-clinical ILD can be seen on imaging with minimal or no symptoms, particularly in patients with anti-SAE, anti-SRP and anti-TIF1γ antibodies, which are associated with severe myositis . Occasionally, ASyS patients might be in this category when extrapulmonary symptoms are predominant . Chest imaging is important in establishing diagnosis, choosing therapy, and estimating prognosis of IIM-ILD ( ). A high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) scan (< 1.5 mm slices) with volumetric scanning of the chest with inspiratory, and expiratory images can help characterize parenchymal disease. Prone images can assist with subtle, sub-pleural changes and distinguish from compression atelectasis or dependent edema. Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) is the most common pattern in C-ILD and is seen in over 50 % of patients with IIM-ILD. It is characterized by peripheral and lower lobe predominant reticulation and ground glass opacities with sub-pleural sparing . Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) is the most common pattern in C-ILD and is seen in over 50 % of patients with IIM-ILD. It is characterized by peripheral and lower lobe predominant reticulation and ground glass opacities with sub-pleural sparing . Organizing pneumonia (OP) pattern is characterized by patchy peripheral or peribronchovascular consolidation and ground glass opacities. The presence of an OP pattern on imaging is associated with a good response to immunosuppression and better outcomes. Concomitant presence of both NSIP and OP patterns are often observed in IIM-ILD. A usual intestinal pneumonia (UIP) pattern is characterized by sub-pleural, predominantly basilar fibrosis, honeycombing, and absence of ground glass opacities. UIP has been reported in 10 to 30% of patients with ASyS, usually in advanced disease . Additional radiographic features have been associated with UIP due to CTD. They include the concentration of fibrosis in the anterior upper lobes, exuberant honeycomb like cysts in the fibrotic parenchyma, lower lobe predominant fibrosis with sharp demarcation with normal lung in the craniocaudal plane. The diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) pattern consists of diffuse ground glass opacities and consolidation. It is commonly seen during an acute exacerbation of C-ILD or in RP-ILD, particularly in patients with anti-MDA5 DM and ASyS. UIP and DAD patterns are associated with poor response to treatment and worse outcomes. The imaging patterns can overlap, evolve, and progress. , Pulmonary function test (PFT) - A restrictive pattern (low total lung capacity and low forced vital capacity [FVC]) on PFT along with a low diffusion of carbon monoxide (DLCO) is the most common finding on PFTs. Patients with mild disease may have an isolated mild reduction in DLCO with normal FVC. Concomitant ILD and emphysema or PH may lead to a reduction in DLCO which is out of proportion to the reduction in FVC reduction. In patients with respiratory muscle weakness, PFTs usually reveal a decreased FVC, normal DLCO, a greater than 20% drop in FVC when laying supine and decreased maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures. Pathology (<xref rid="SD1" ref-type="supplementary-material">Figure S1</xref>)- Lung biopsy is rarely needed to establish a diagnosis of IIM-ILD with classical clinical, radiographic, and serological presentations. Occasionally, it may be needed to rule out malignancy. NSIP is the most common pathological finding. A UIP pattern is seen in a minority of patients. Both NSIP and UIP may be associated with an acute pathology, either DAD or OP. Pulmonary hypertension (PH) has been reported in 8 to 10% of patients with ASyS and is associated with decreased survival . Echocardiogram is used as a screening test to determine if further work-up for PH is warranted, but the clinician needs to maintain a high clinical suspicion as echocardiography in patients with parenchymal lung disease may be inaccurate. The diagnosis of PH requires confirmation by right heart catheterization. In patients with concomitant advanced ILD, PH is classified as World Symposium for Pulmonary Hypertension (WSPH) group 3 disease. However, pulmonary arterial hypertension (WSPH group 1) can also occur in IIM . Rarely, PH can be a consequence of myocarditis, inflammatory infiltration in the cardiac conduction system and replacement fibrosis (WSPH group 2). Patients may present with angina, dysrhythmias, or congestive heart failure. Cardiac MRI is a sensitive technique that can detect mild inflammation in the myocardium. , Respiratory muscle disease- Respiratory muscle (diaphragm, intercostal muscles) weakness can present with dyspnea and orthopnea and can progress to hypercapnic respiratory failure if severe. Isolated respiratory muscle involvement is rare. However, subclinical diaphragm weakness is common and can be seen in up to 75% of patients, often with mild symptoms or normal PFT. Dyspnea in the absence of parenchymal or pulmonary vascular disease should trigger work-up for muscle weakness. Diaphragmatic ultrasound is a promising, non-invasive method to assess diaphragm function by measuring diaphragm dome excursion and diaphragm thickness. It can accurately measure diaphragm function in other neuromuscular diseases, but clinical utility in IIM is yet to be established. Aspiration- Dysphagia can occur due to pharyngeal muscle weakness or esophageal dysmotility. In the EuroMyositis registry, 26% of patients with ASyS and 53% of those with OM reported dysphagia . This can lead to aspiration pneumonia or pneumonitis. Video-fluoroscopic swallowing study and manometry can be used to evaluate dysphagia. Musculoskeletal manifestations: (<xref rid="SD1" ref-type="supplementary-material">Figure S2</xref>) Myopathy is a hallmark feature of IIM. The characteristic presentation is symmetric, proximal muscle weakness with hip and thigh muscles being the most frequently affected areas. Common symptoms are difficulty standing from a seated position, climbing steps, or raising arms overhead. Neck extensor muscle weakness can cause head drop and pharyngeal muscle weakness may result in dysphagia and voice change. Myalgia and muscle tenderness are common with ASyS. A detailed neurologic examination is critical in determining the severity and distribution of muscle weakness and to rule out myositis mimics. In patients with ASyS, lung disease in the absence of or preceding myositis by months is typical . Absence of myopathy is most often seen in anti-MDA5 DM but can also be associated with other MSAs. CADM patients are at higher risk of developing ILD compared to classic DM patients, and CADM is considered a predictor of RP-ILD. - Diagnostic work up for myopathy includes a variable combination of muscle enzymes, muscle magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), electromyography, and muscle biopsy. Creatine kinase (CK) is the most sensitive measurable muscle enzyme and can be used to monitor treatment responses and relapses. Other non-specific biomarkers of muscle injury include aldolase, lactate dehydrogenase and aminotransferases. Bilateral thigh MRI using a myositis protocol (T1-weighted imaging, fluid-sensitive T2W with fat suppression or short-tau inversion recovery sequence) can be used to identify early stages of myositis and target areas for a muscle biopsy. Findings include edema of muscle fibers, alteration in muscle signal intensity and in later stages presence of fatty infiltration, fibrosis, or muscle atrophy. These changes are not specific to myositis and can also be seen in injuries, muscle infarction, denervation, or rhabdomyolysis. - Electromyography can distinguish myopathy from neuropathic causes of weakness. Myopathy is characterized by polyphasic motor unit action potentials that are of short-duration, low amplitude on voluntary activation and prominent muscle membrane irritability at rest. Electromyography is not diagnostic of myositis, as similar findings can occur in infectious, toxic, metabolic or degenerative myopathies. It can guide muscle biopsy, but muscle biopsy should not be performed on a muscle that has recently undergone electromyography testing. - Arthritis or arthralgia is seen in 90% of IIM patients and is the presenting symptom in 30% of ASyS patients. Three general patterns of joint involvement are seen: i)- symmetrical, non-erosive, polyarthritis affecting the hand joints and knees (~60%), ii) isolated joint arthralgia (25%), and iii) subluxing arthropathy affecting the distal interphalangeal joints (15%). Plain radiographs typically demonstrate non-destructive arthropathy, although erosive arthritis has been reported in a minority of cases. Skin manifestations: (<xref rid="F3" ref-type="fig">Figure 3</xref>) The presence of classical skin findings, on history or examination, can be helpful in establishing a diagnosis; however, the appearance of skin manifestations can be impacted by the individual patient’s skin tone. Several pathognomonic DM skin findings have been described and can be seen in various combinations in IIM: Heliotrope rash (periorbital violaceous erythema commonly with edema) Gottron papules (erythematous-to-violaceous papules and plaques, overlying metacarpo-phalangeal and interphalangeal joints) Gottron sign (erythematous macules or patches over extensor surfaces of joints) Shawl sign (erythema over posterior shoulders, neck, and upper back) V sign (erythema over lower anterior neck and upper chest) Nailfold changes (Periungual nailfold erythema, telangiectasia, punctate cuticular hemorrhage) Holster sign (symmetric poikiloderma of hips and lateral thighs) Mechanic’s hands- non-pruritic, hyperkeratotic eruptions on the lateral surface of fingers. Common in ASyS patients. Most of the skin lesions are pruritic or burning and some can be photosensitive. Skin hypo/hyperpigmentation, atrophy, and telangiectasia resulting in poikiloderma can occur, especially on the upper chest and lateral upper arms. Patients with anti-MDA5 DM may develop relatively specific skin features, including skin erosions, ulcerations over joints or on digits, and tender palmar papules. Lesional skin biopsies can be helpful in diagnosing patients with CADM and may prevent the need for muscle biopsy in patients with other IIMs. Characteristic histologic findings include interface dermatitis with dyskeratosis, increased dermal mucin, chronic perivascular inflammation, and vascular dilatation and/or damage. Nail-fold capillaroscopy can aid in diagnosis and prognostication. Findings include enlarged capillaries, disorganized vascular array, capillary loss, and scleroderma-like patterns . Furthermore, cancer is a leading cause of death in adults with IIM. , Various cancers including lung, ovarian, colorectal, breast, lymphoma and nasopharyngeal cancer are amongst the most common forms. The risk and screening strategies vary significantly based on the disease phenotype and antibody profile. Patients with DM (anti-TIF1γ, NXP-2 ab) with age >40 years at IIM onset, dysphagia and cutaneous necrosis are at the highest risk for having an underlying malignancy followed by patients with PM, IMNM or CADM, who are at intermediate risk. Patients with ASA (Anti-Jo1, Non-Jo1 Ab), MAA or Anti-SRP antibody with features of Raynaud phenomenon, inflammatory arthropathy and ILD are low risk. Based on risk stratification, screening for occult malignancies with imaging, cancer markers, whole body positron emission tomography scans should be considered. Classification criteria of IIM (<xref rid="T2" ref-type="table">Table 2</xref>) Bohan and Peter provided classification criteria for DM in 1975, which was widely used for 40 years. , They included characteristic DM rashes and the need to exclude other causes of myopathy but did not mention pulmonary manifestations. Patients with anti-Jo-1 Ab were recognized as having a distinct phenotype termed ASyS in the early 90s. , Since then, IIMs have been further classified based on clinical manifestations and antibody profiles. In 2017, the first validated classification criteria of IIM by the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) and European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) were developed and provided the probability of having IIM. The criteria include age of onset, pattern of muscle weakness, muscle enzyme elevation, muscle biopsy findings, presence of rash, and anti-Jo-1 Ab. It did not include ILD, or non-Jo-1 antibodies. The criteria also do not define ASyS as a distinct IIM subtype. There are active efforts for establishing a revised classification criteria for IIM and separate classification criteria for ASyS. Currently, criteria suggested by Solomon et al and Connor et al based-on expert opinion, are widely used to establish a diagnosis of ASyS. Presence of anti-synthetase antibodies with any one or two clinical features (ILD, IIM, RP, skin changes) can be considered adequate for diagnosing ASyS , . Management Immunosuppression is the mainstay of treatment of IIM-ILD targeting several pathways. As with most rare diseases, few clinical trials exist, and treatment varies based on clinical presentation and center preference. The American College of Rheumatology is finalizing guidelines for management of CTD-ILD, which appear consistent with our approach outlined here . Patients with RP-ILD need early, aggressive, combination anti-inflammatory therapy. Patients with C-ILD can be treated in “step-up” escalation of therapy over months. Patients with subclinical disease can be monitored without therapy but require close follow-up. Treatment decisions are based on expert opinion, experience, the “clinical gestalt” of individual treatment teams and require multi-disciplinary collaboration. Table 3 summarizes our recommendations on starting dosing, common adverse events, and monitoring of several immunosuppressant agents used in patients with IIM-ILD. Corticosteroids Corticosteroids (CS) have been the first-line treatment for pulmonary and extra-pulmonary manifestations of IIM for decades. A meta-analysis of patients with IIM-ILD (45% ASyS, 40 % DM), reviewed the impact of various treatment strategies. Six studies in the analysis included 124 patients who received CS monotherapy. A significant improvement was reported in 89% of the patients. However, the meta-analysis had several limitations and none of the included studies were controlled. Most studies evaluating other therapies for IIM-ILD have patients on background CS, thus limiting data on using a “steroid-free” approach. In clinical practice, most patients are started on CS at time of diagnosis either as a single agent or in combination with a steroid-sparing agent. Advantages of CS include quick onset, low cost, and physician experience. However, long-term use of CS carries significant morbidity. Given the significant morbidity associated with long-term CS, we advocate to start them in conjunction with a steroid-sparing agent early in the course of disease. Anti-metabolites Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), methotrexate, and azathioprine inhibit lymphocyte activation and proliferation by inhibiting DNA synthesis through various mechanisms. In patients with IIM-ILD, they are commonly used as first-line steroid sparing agent due to good patient tolerance and favorable adverse effect profiles. However, data are limited to retrospective studies. In a single-center retrospective study of 125 CTD-ILD patients (32 with IIM), MMF led to improvement or stabilization of disease across various underlying CTDs. Patients with UIP pathology demonstrated stabilization and those with non-UIP had improvement in lung function. In a retrospective review of patients with IIM-ILD, both MMF and azathioprine led to improvement or stabilization of lung function (FVC improvement 3.6% in MMF group, 3.3% in azathioprine group) and a significant reduction in prednisone dose (6.9 mg in MMF group, 15 mg in azathioprine group) at 24 months. The rate of medication adverse effects was slightly higher in the azathioprine group . Mira-Avendano et al. compared cyclophosphamide, azathioprine and MMF as second-line agents in steroid-refractory IIM-ILD and reported that all three led to an improvement in FVC, DLCO and dyspnea scores at 12 months. We recommend testing for thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) deficiency in patients taking azathioprine as TPMT intermediate metabolizers require lower doses, and poor metabolizers should not receive azathioprine. Methotrexate has been efficacious in treating myositis and has a steroid-sparing effect; however, data in ILD is scarce. Casal-Dominguez compared methotrexate and azathioprine monotherapy in 102 ASyS patients. Both drugs led to improvement in muscle strength, reduced CS dose requirement, and a similar rate of adverse effects. However, 4% of patients developed methotrexate pneumonitis. While the use of methotrexate remains a viable alternative to other anti-metabolites drugs, clinicians must be aware of the risk of pneumonitis. Calcineurin Inhibitors (CNI) The CNIs, tacrolimus and cyclosporine, inhibit T cell function by inhibiting the enzyme calcineurin and impairing transcription of cytokines such as interlukin-2. In a randomized controlled trial (RCT) in patients with IIM- ILD, Fujisawa et al. compared the use of tacrolimus and cyclosporine as first add-on agents in 58 patients with IIM-ILD (47% CADM, 33% DM, 20% PM. Patients in both groups showed similar improvement in FVC (19% tacrolimus, 16% cyclosporine) and DLCO (14% tacrolimus, 9% cyclosporine). This trial demonstrated efficacy of CNI as first-line agents with CS but was not designed to compare them to other treatments . Therefore, CNIs can be used as first- or second-line steroid-sparing agents. The choice between tacrolimus and cyclosporine is physician-dependent, with no evidence of superiority for either agent. Rituximab Rituximab is an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody which leads to peripheral B cell depletion. The RECITAL RCT compared rituximab and cyclophosphamide as second-line agents in 101 CTD-ILD patients (44 with IIM-ILD). Both rituximab and cyclophosphamide increased the median FVC at 24 weeks (94 ml rituximab, 99 ml cyclophosphamide) and 48 weeks (112 ml rituximab, 138 ml cyclophosphamide). DLCO, six min walk distance (6MWD), and quality of life also improved in both groups. The cyclophosphamide group had more total adverse effects but similar serious adverse events. This RCT demonstrated that most patients treated with second line rituximab or cyclophosphamide improve, with similar efficacy of both agents. Retrospective studies have shown similar efficacy of cyclophosphamide and rituximab and a better adverse effect profile with rituximab. In a systematic review of patients with anti-MDA5 ILD, 71% of patients responded to rituximab as a second- or third-line agent. Rituximab can be used as a second-line agent in refractory disease. Cyclophosphamide Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating agent, commonly used for cancer chemotherapy. It is used for induction in life-threatening autoimmune conditions due to its rapid and profound immune suppression. In addition to data from the RECITAL RCT (see above), similar findings were seen in a systematic review of five studies analyzing cyclophosphamide use in IIM- ILD patients (55 % anti-Jo-1 Ab). In this review, 71% of patients had improvement in FVC, 69% had improvement in DLCO, and 67% had improvement in chest CT findings. Cyclophosphamide can be administered up to six months in severe or RP-ILD, with transition to less toxic agents once disease is in remission. In a single-center, open-label trial with retrospective controls, Chen et al. studied the efficacy of tofacitinib as a first-line steroid-sparing agent in 18 patients with anti-MDA5 ILD, compared to 32 historical controls. The six-month survival was 100% in the tofacitinib group compared to 78% in controls. They reported an improvement in FVC, DLCO and chest CT scores in the tofacitinib group. Fan et al. compared tofacitinib with tacrolimus in a retrospective study of patients with anti-MDA5 DM. Over 50% of patients had RP-ILD. Lower mortality in tofacitinib group was seen at six months (38.5% vs 62.9%) and one year (44.0% vs 65.7%). It has also shown efficacy in patients with disease refractory to other agents. Tofacitinib is orally dosed and can be used as a second- or third-line agent in anti-MDA5 DM. Intravenous immune globulin (IVIg) IVIg is purified from pooled human plasma, consisting of monomeric Immunoglobulin G. IVIg has shown efficacy in treating DM patients, with decreased disease activity compared to placebo. In IIM-ILD, data are limited. In a retrospective study, 17 ASyS patients (80% with refractory disease) were treated with IVIg for six months and followed for two years; FVC % and DLCO % increased, and prednisone dose decreased . Most patients were on concomitant immune suppression. The lack of a control group limits the ability to conclude efficacy. The main indication for IVIg in IIM is to treat extra-pulmonary disease and as second- or third-line therapy in RP- ILD. The side effect profile of IVIg and lack of immunosuppression makes it an attractive add on therapy in patients with severe lung disease or in patients where active infections have not been ruled out. Anti-fibrotic therapy Nintedanib and pirfenidone have demonstrated efficacy in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. The INBUILD RCT studied the efficacy of nintedanib in 663 patients with progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF). In this study, 25 % of the included patients had CTD-ILD. Nintedanib slowed the rate of progression in the entire cohort. Data from patients with IIM-ILD were not reported separately . In a single center, prospective study of patients with IIM-ILD, 39 patients on nintedanib were compared to those receiving standard-of-care therapy. Patients in the nintedanib group had a lower RP-ILD risk and better survival compared to controls. In the 2022 American Thoracic Society guidelines for PPF, nintedanib is recommended for PPF patients. Pirfenidone did not meet its primary endpoint in patients with PPF in the RELIEF trial. However, the study had to be stopped due to poor recruitment and futility. The determination of disease progression can be challenging in ILD, particularly in IIM-ILD. Clinicians should give a trial of adequate immunosuppressive treatment with step-up as indicated after the initial diagnosis before using antifibrotics. Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) TPE can decrease the levels of autoantibodies, cytokines, and immune complexes. Data on TPE in IIM-ILD is limited to case series. In a retrospective study of 11 patients who underwent TPE for anti-MDA 5 ILD, survival was 90% in the TPE group compared to 50 % in the non-TPE group. With limited data, TPE continues to be used as a salvage therapy for RP-ILD. Lung transplantation Lung transplantation is an option for selected patients with end-stage lung disease. Patients with progressive disease despite appropriate therapy, need for supplemental oxygen, progressive fibrotic disease, and RP- ILD should be considered for transplant evaluation. In addition to standard issues of candidate selection, extra-pulmonary manifestations of IIM can impact candidacy and post-transplant outcomes. Active myositis can affect rehabilitation potential, ventilator weaning and risk of aspiration. Therefore, it needs to be quiescent before transplant referral. Post-transplant outcomes in IIM-ILD are comparable to those for other indications in US and European cohorts. Timely referral to an experienced transplant center can help improve the likelihood of a successful transplant. Pulmonary rehabilitation Pulmonary rehabilitation is a comprehensive intervention for patients with chronic lung disease that includes exercise training and education, usually in an outpatient setting. A Cochrane review of 16 trials in patients with ILD demonstrated that pulmonary rehabilitation helped to improve 6MWD, dyspnea, and quality of life, with no significant adverse effects. This treatment modality remains underutilized despite high reward and low risk profile. Referral should be considered in all symptomatic patients with IIM-ILD. Infection prevention and prophylaxis Patients on immune suppression are at increased risk for infectious complications. Prophylaxis for pneumocystis pneumonia with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or an alternate regimen is started in patients on two immune-suppression medications or those on high dose corticosteroids (greater than 20 mg/ day prednisone for one month). Age and location specific immunization prior initiation of immune suppression as well as seasonal annual immunization is strongly recommended. Management of PH In patients with WSPH group I PAH, treatment according to the latest WSPH guidelines for group 1 disease should be pursued. Immune suppression has been reported to be beneficial in observational studies in patients with systematic lupus erythematosus and MCTD associated PH. However there is no supporting data in patients with IIM related PH. In patients with WSPH Group 3 PH due to ILD, inhaled treprostinil is recommended as it has shown to increase 6MWD (mean increase 31m), improve biomarkers of right heart failure (nt-pro BNP) and decrease the incidence of clinical deterioration (22 % vs 33%). Management of respiratory muscle weakness Aggressive immune modulation with high-dose steroids, IVIg and other agents should be initiated depending on the degree of muscle weakness. Patients need to be monitored closely for worsening disease with measurements of negative inspiratory force and vital capacity. A negative inspiratory force of less than 30 cmH2O and FVC of less than 20ml/kg may warrant monitoring in an intensive care unit setting. Patients may progress to respiratory failure and require noninvasive or invasive mechanical ventilation. Management in this situation is similar to other neuromuscular diseases affecting the respiratory system. Noninvasive ventilation can help improve hypercapnia, sleep quality and quality of life in patients with chronic hypoventilation. Treatment approach (<xref rid="F4" ref-type="fig">Figure 4</xref>) Our management approach is based on disease acuity, severity, and co-morbidities. Specific antibody profiles can help predict clinical course, but we do not use them in isolation to make treatment decisions. In patients with incidental, mild, or subclinical disease with no symptoms and normal pulmonary physiology, a “wait and watch” approach can be adopted. We closely monitor for the development of symptoms and measure PFT every 3 to 6 months to look for any signs of progression. In C-ILD patients, we use a “step- up” approach starting with a single agent, monitoring response, and stepping up treatment over weeks or months. First line therapy includes moderate dose CS (prednisone 0.5-1 mg/kg), with tapering over 2-3 months to the lowest tolerated dose. Depending on severity, we often start an antimetabolite within weeks. We use rituximab or CNIs as second-line agents either alone or in combination with IVIG. Cyclophosphamide can be used as a third-line agent in refractory disease. Anti-fibrotic medications are added in PPF if there is progression on optimal anti-inflammatory therapies. In patients with RP-ILD we start with early “aggressive” therapy to induce remission, followed by a “step down” approach once the disease is quiescent. The favored regimen varies based on experience and institution but includes a combination of high dose CS and one or two immunomodulators (CNI, cyclophosphamide, rituximab, IVIg and tofacitinib). Lung transplantation should be considered early in patients with single-organ disease and respiratory failure. Several retrospective studies have reported the utility of combination Immune suppression in patients with anti-MDA5 ILD . Prognosis Estimated one-year survival in patients with IIM-ILD is over 90%- and ten-year cumulative survival is ~80% .When compared to patients with IPF, survival is significantly better in IIM-ILD. Patients with anti-MDA5 DM continue to have a high short-term mortality, with 75% one-year survival , , .Acute exacerbations of ILD carry a high short-term mortality irrespective of underlying IIM. The overall age-adjusted mortality rate for IIM-ILD in the US has been stable for the past two decades .Factors associated with lower survival are anti- MDA5 positivity, older age at onset, RP-ILD, poor response to therapy, elevated inflammatory markers, UIP pattern, malignancy, and concomitant PH , . Conclusion and Future directions IIMs are a common cause of chronic and RP-ILD, often with isolated lung disease. Recognition of IIM as a cause of ILD is essential since most patients respond to initial immunosuppressive treatment. The widespread availability of MAA/MSA testing can help improve diagnosis and phenotyping of this disease. Notably, there is lack of reliable biomarkers to guide therapy and monitor the clinical response.

Conclusion and Future directions IIMs are a common cause of chronic and RP-ILD, often with isolated lung disease. Recognition of IIM as a cause of ILD is essential since most patients respond to initial immunosuppressive treatment. The widespread availability of MAA/MSA testing can help improve diagnosis and phenotyping of this disease. Notably, there is lack of reliable biomarkers to guide therapy and monitor the clinical response. Further, better diagnostic criteria for IIM should recognize isolated IIM-ILD (“pneumo-myositis”) and ASyS. The guidelines may help standardize diagnosis and aid in treatment trials. Several treatments continue to be investigated in patients with IIM, with many ongoing clinical trials. Immune modulators targeting various pathways are being repurposed for use in IIM-ILD. Case reports have shown benefit with daratumumab (anti CD38 ab), basiliximab (IL-2 receptor antagonist), tocilizumab (IL-6 antagonist), abatacept (selective costimulation modulator), anakinra (interleukin-1 receptor antagonist) and ruxolitinib (JAK inhibitor) amongst others , .The infusion of chimeric antigen receptor T cells that recognize CD19 + B cells can lead to their depletion and an “immune reset”. This therapy has shown promise in inducing remission in patients with refractory SLE . Two recent case reports demonstrated remission in patients with refractory ASyS with chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy , .While this is encouraging, data is scant, and this is still considered investigational.
